items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [Fast Company] 31 leaders on whether they still want to talk about AI
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

On the morning, noon, and nightly news. By the watercooler, virtual or in real life. In boardrooms and school board meetings. At the dinner table or gatherings with friends and family. Artificial intelligence continues to dominate discussions across work, home, school, and social life.

We asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council whether they love talking about AI or would rather never hear about AI again—and why? Below, 31 leaders weigh in on whether they’ve hit “let’s talk about AI” burnout or still on the bandwagon. They also share what conversations around AI matter least and most.

1. CONVERSATIONS ON HOW IT ALLOWS US TO STRETCH

I love the conversation around AI and think it’s incredibly important. For all of history, new technologies have emerged and there have been people who feared them and people who embraced them. Resisting AI, or any new technology for that matter, isn’t going to make it go away . . . but it will cause you to fall behind. To embrace AI means more than just automating tasks. It allows us to stretch beyond what’s in front of us and completely reimagine our work. There was a time people feared the internet. Now, we can’t imagine life without it. I see the same potential for AI and whatever inevitably comes next. That excites me. — Glen Tullman, Transcarent

2. TIRED OF AI, BUT NOT DONE LEARNING

I am tired of talking about AI. But that’s not a good enough reason not to keep talking about it, and more importantly, reading and learning about it. The technology is here to stay. The question is how do we bring humanity to it so we drive it versus it driving us. — Phillip Haid, Public Inc.

3. LOVE DISCUSSION OF DEEPER AI QUESTIONS

I love talking about AI because it exposes a deeper question: Why is work still so hard to navigate? Enterprises are extraordinary achievements of specialization, but that specialization creates a tax on work with more systems, handoffs, and institutional knowledge for employees to decipher. The enterprise needs coherence more than it needs another isolated intelligence. AI’s promise is not more content or another interface. It is less distance between intent and outcome, giving people more time for judgment, creativity, and care. — Bhavin Shah, ServiceNow

4. ENJOY TALKING ABOUT PRACTICAL USE CASES

I enjoy talking about AI, especially when the conversation is focused on practical use cases, not just hype. Our team is always looking for ways to help nonprofits punch above their weight, and AI is a powerful tool to help them do just that. Internally, we’re now using AI to handle about 60% of our routine support tickets and releasing product updates 50% faster, giving our team more time for the work that matters most. At the end of the day, AI is just another tool in our toolbox, and conversations about how we can use this new tool safely, responsibly, and effectively are always welcome in my book. — Max Friedman, Givebutter

5. TIRED OF ABSTRACT HYPE, MORE INTO REAL IMPACT STORIES

I am tired of talking about or hearing about AI in the abstract, from announcements of new “AI chiefs” to press releases on new AI products. What I do want to hear about is real impact and outcomes—customers that have seen transformative impact from this use of this technology. — Scott Brighton, Bonterra

6. NEVER TIRED TALKING ABOUT HOW TO UNLOCK AI

I love it, because the question has changed. It’s no longer, “Should we use AI?” Employees already answered that themselves with their curiosity and newfound efficiencies. The question is, “How do we make AI safe enough to say ‘yes’?” That’s the conversation I have every day. Chief information officers and chief information security officers need visibility and control over every prompt, agent, and AI session across browsers, desktops, and devices. Getting to talk about AI as something we unlock, not fear, is a conversation I’ll never get tired of. — Steve Tchejeyan, Island

7. LOVE DISCUSSING WHAT AI FORCES US TO ANSWER

I love talking about AI, honestly, more than I expected to a few years ago. What keeps me hooked isn’t the technology itself. It’s the question it forces every leader to answer: What do you actually stand for, now that a large language model will amplify it at scale? That’s the most interesting conversation I’ve had in decades of doing this work. The day I’d want to stop talking about AI is the day people stop asking what it means to be human alongside it, and we’re nowhere close to that. — Carol Cone, Carol Cone ON PURPOSE

8. LOVE MARKET CHANGING DISCUSSIONS

I love talking about AI because it is changing something fundamental about marketing: how people discover and understand brands. Increasingly, people will ask AI what an organization is known for before they ever visit its website or see a campaign. You cannot control what AI says about your brand, but you can dramatically improve the evidence from which it forms its answer. So, discoverability, credibility, and accumulated evidence are more important than ever. — R. Ethan Braden, Texas A&M University

9. CONVERSATIONS ABOUT HOW TO OPERATIONALIZE IT

I love talking about AI, and I look forward to the day it sounds as odd as bragging about using electricity. The day nobody in security mentions AI, because it is simply how the work gets done, is the day we succeeded in giving security teams what they need to fight AI-driven attacks. We are past the question of whether AI works in security. The conversations now are about how to operationalize it today. When a transformation is moving this fast, a lot of those conversations are still necessary. But not for long. — Lior Div, 7AI

10. NEVER HEARING ABOUT IT AGAIN ISN’T AN OPTION

We’re still in the early chapters of the AI story, and it’s one of the most transformational, polarizing shifts I’ve seen. We’re in the FAFO stage, so never hearing about it again isn’t an option. I want to hear more about its additive impact: equitable healthcare access, faster drug discovery, fraud detection, and climate modeling that reduces disaster impact. I’m in awe of the next generation and how they use AI to get more out of their day. I won’t pretend I’m not worried about AI’s worst-case version. But I’m encouraged to hear how it’s pushing us back toward human judgment and critical thinking. — Tyler Perry, Mission North

11. IMPORTANT TOPIC ABOUT CHANGE AND HUMAN AMPLIFICATION

I love talking about AI because it’s a force driving change today. It’s a reality, regardless of how you feel about technology. Pandora’s box has been opened. The real story isn’t about replacement. It’s about human amplification. Technology is a tool; it doesn’t replace us. I use AI daily as a thought partner to structure ideas, speed up research, and get tasks done. AI models are becoming a commodity—flooding the internet with homogenized content. Referenceable, human-created content becomes exponentially more valuable. AI is incredible for instant retrieval, but human judgment and real-world context are what build true understanding. — Tony Grimminck, Scribd, Inc.

12. FOCUS DISCUSSIONS ON REAL PROBLEMS AI CAN SOLVE

I enjoy talking about AI when the conversation starts with the problem, not the technology. We’ve used AI at my company since 2016 to solve very human challenges, like matching older adults with the right caregivers and creating more stable jobs for home care workers. My advice to leaders: Don’t start by asking where you can use AI. Start with a real problem worth solving, then determine how AI can be leveraged to solve it. — Seth Sternberg, Honor

13. CONVERSATIONS AROUND PEOPLE-CENTERED USE ARE EXCITING

I’m curious about AI and genuinely interested in where it can take us, particularly when it comes to helping people uncover insights and make better-informed decisions. At the same time, I don’t believe technology can replace human judgment, experience, or relationships. The most exciting conversations, for me, are about how we can use AI thoughtfully while keeping people at the center. — Liz Hershfield, COTTON USA

14. LOVE TALKING ABOUT THE REAL IMPACT OF AI

I love talking about AI, especially when the conversation moves beyond hype and focuses on real impact. It can strengthen communication, make high-quality knowledge more discoverable, streamline creative work, and give individuals and small teams access to powerful capabilities. But I believe it should be used with judgment: not as a replacement for human thinking, experience, or sensitivity, but as a tool that requires context, responsibility, and an authentic voice. AI is most valuable when it helps us ask better questions, make better decisions, and communicate more clearly. — Manuel Freire-Garabal, Gioya Health Education Institution

15. TIME TO DISCUSS WHETHER WE’RE PREPARED TO USE IT

I talk about it constantly, but carefully, in my industry. Most AI discourse in education still centers on the tools. The urgent question is teacher readiness. Adoption is moving faster than training can keep pace with, and educators are being handed AI mandates with no framework for using it responsibly in a classroom. That gap is where students get shortchanged, not from the technology itself. So no, I don’t want to stop talking about AI. I want the conversation to move past the tools and onto whether we’re preparing the adults in the room to use it well. — Kellie Lauth, MindSpark

16. CONVERSATIONS ON AI ACHIEVEMENTS ARE MOST INTERESTING

Honestly, I’d love to hear less about AI in general and more about what it has achieved. Most conversations are still stuck on the hype. The interesting ones focus on how an AI model actually understands the business it is serving. At my company, that means a conversation grounded in retail shelves, reducing waste, preventing stockouts, and improving profitability. — Are Traasdahl, Crisp

17. LOVE WITNESSING REAL-WORLD AI APPLICATIONS

I love that I am witnessing real-world applications to improve operational efficiency and speed time to market. We use AI across the organization. But core to our business, we use it to build software, run our predictable energy management tools, and make commercial charging more reliable, efficient, and predictable. Our energy management system optimizes how available power is allocated based on site capacity, vehicle demand, and operating needs. We also use charger telemetry to identify potential equipment issues before they disrupt a session. We also use AI in legal, financial planning, site build out analysis, and customer support. — Patrick Macdonald-King, Greenlane

18. LOVE DISCUSSING ADVANCEMENTS RELATED TO PEOPLE, SKILLS

I love talking about AI and hearing about the latest advancements, especially when the conversation comes back to people and skills. I don’t believe AI simply “does it for you” or replaces jobs. It raises the bar for what “good” looks like, which makes deep expertise even more important. You still need people who understand the work well enough to direct it. My advice is don’t let AI become an excuse to stop building real skills on your team. — Tigran Sloyan, CodeSignal

19. NEED DISCUSSIONS ON HOW IT’S SHAPING THE WORLD FOR CHILDREN

Plenty of AI conversations are about the technology and the business innovation, and I find those genuinely interesting. But I could talk endlessly about something I think is much bigger: the world AI is shaping for our children. By the time we get to the headline about AI and childhood, the shape will be pretty much set—which is exactly why we need to have the conversations now. — Michele Walsh, UNICEF USA

20. FROM “WHAT CAN WE DO?” TO “WHAT SHOULD WE DO?”

I’ve always been an early adopter of technologies and gadgets, and AI is no exception. When ChatGPT first launched in November of 2022, I spent the holidays experimenting and showing it to everyone in my family who’d listen. In the years since, I’ve tried countless tools, built agents, tried my hand at vibe-coding, and worked it into our operations and workflows in my marketing firm. But as we come up on the fourth anniversary of ChatGPT, I’m feeling the fatigue of constant experimentation. I want to get back to the work of providing real value, not just volume and speed. I’m asking not just “What can we do?” but “What should we do?” — Lisa Larson-Kelley, Quantious

21. LOVE DISCUSSION THE EXPANSION OF HUMAN CAPACITY

I love discussing what AI makes possible, not AI as an end in itself. Its real value isn’t mimicking human creativity. It’s removing friction, surfacing patterns, and accelerating exploration. In design, that translates to rapid spatial analysis, testing more scenarios, and cutting repetitive tasks. The leadership question isn’t “What can AI do?” but “What can our people do better because AI is handling the rest?” It’s about expanding human capacity, not replacing humanity. — Susan Watts, SPACECRAFT

22. EXCITED TO TALK ABOUT HOW AI RESHAPES INDUSTRIES

I love it. I’m excited about AI’s potential to expand what people and organizations can achieve. We’re at a point where leaders have an opportunity to rethink how work gets done, how decisions are made, and even what their businesses could look like if they were being built today. That’s a mindset we’re embracing as we explore what it means to reinvent a 170-year-old company for an AI-native world. I’m equally energized by what I’m seeing beyond our own walls, learning how other leaders are approaching the technology and how AI is reshaping industries in ways we’re only beginning to understand. That’s a conversation I’ll never tire of. — Michael Lefenfeld, Hexion

23. THE AI QUESTION IS A PRACTICAL ONE

I love talking about AI. Our 2026 Estate Planning Report found the share of Americans who trust AI more than a human attorney for estate planning guidance jumped from 20% to 30% in one year, and 46% of Gen Z agree. The objection changed too. In 2025, people asked whether AI should be involved at all. Now they ask practical questions: Will it get my situation right, and is my data secure? That is real progress, because practical questions can be answered. We answer them by pairing AI guidance with attorney oversight, and I think that combination is where every professional service is headed. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will

24. CRUCIAL TO DISCUSS WHAT IT COSTS TO RUN

AI isn’t going anywhere, so the real question isn’t whether we join the conversation, but rather are we conscious of what it costs to run it. Every large language model depends on a data center that consumes enormous amounts of water and power, often in a very wasteful manner. At my company, we’re utilizing AI internally through platforms like REDSTAR, an AI system for real-time water treatment and monitoring, while building partnerships to bring closed-loop cooling water treatment and reuse to the data centers powering the AI industry in the United States. AI is a huge opportunity for anyone who uses it and done right it also doesn’t have to cost us the planet. — Kevin Gast, VVater

25. FASCINATED BY WHAT AI REVEALS ABOUT OURSELVES

I am fascinated by AI and love talking about it. When we talk about what we want from or fear about AI, we are talking about what we want from and fear about ourselves and our trust of humanity. Do we understand the best human impacts? Do we trust ourselves to not destroy ourselves? Historically these questions have surfaced around other technologies like splitting the atom. Each time, how we navigate the impact and use of new technologies usually says more about ourselves than anything about the technology itself. — Troy Thompson, SmithGroup

26. AI CAN CREATE GOOSEBUMPS, BUT CAN’T FEEL THEM

What excites me about AI isn’t the buzz surrounding it. It’s the barriers it can break down and the possibilities it can open. AI is an extraordinary tool—but the tool is never the idea. And technology will never be more powerful than the humanity guiding it. At its best, AI gives creative people more freedom to imagine, experiment, and bring ideas to life. It can expand what’s possible, but it can never replace the human instinct, emotion, and truth that make creativity matter. It can create an image of goosebumps. But it will never know what it feels like to have them. — David Angelo, David&Goliath

27. LOVE LEARNING HOW PEOPLE ARE USING IT

I love learning what others are doing with AI. I find it fascinating hearing what everyday people are building to improve their lives. Just last week, a friend told me he built an AI agent to help him plan future vacations that are optimized to what he loves, right down to the type of hotel to book, restaurants to explore, etc. — Ed Mitzen, The Business For Good Foundation

28. CHANGES HOW I THINK ABOUT POSSIBILITIES

I choose to be optimistic about AI and I enjoy talking about it. Almost every week, I come across a new development or possibility that changes how I think about what it can enable. Avoiding the conversation right now feels a bit like being against the internet in the 1990s. — Erik Herrström, STUDIO HERRSTRÖM

29. ENJOY LEARNING RATHER THAN TALKING ABOUT IT

I enjoy learning about it more than I enjoy talking about it. I’m a decades-long career technologist who has witnessed remarkable transformations, but none more fast-paced or broad-reaching than AI. It is not a fad. Ignoring it will leave you and your organization behind in a blink. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps

30. LOVE TALKING ABOUT PUTTING POWER IN PEOPLE’S HANDS

I love talking about AI when it’s about putting real power in people’s hands—helping people get faster, personalized, and more affordable healthcare experiences. I’m not interested in AI as just another way to optimize margins or protect incumbents. The only AI that matters is the kind that improves people’s lives and outcomes. — Owen Tripp, Included Health

31. PRODUCTIVE CONVERSATIONS ABOUT WORK AND CONNECTION

I love talking about AI and how it is reshaping recruitment. I am tired of hearing how AI is going to destroy the world, because I think the more productive conversation is about how we can use it responsibly to improve the way people work and connect with opportunities. — Paul Toomey, Geographic Solutions

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.content_html:

Government agencies in New York’s Broome County, Idaho and South Africa took websites offline or replaced them with simplified versions on Friday in response to warnings about critical flaws in PHP, the programming language used by nearly 70% of websites whose programming language can be identified. The FBI said the vulnerabilities could let attackers remotely run code in PHP and potentially compromise data and networks. The PHP Foundation released patches and instructions on Wednesday, and the FBI urged organizations to update affected systems or take them offline until they can be secured. Idaho officials said they were prioritizing internet-facing systems and sites supporting public safety and essential government services; Broome County and South Africa’s Presidency had not said in their statements when their websites would be restored. Broome County directed residents seeking county services to call 607-778-8000.

PHP’s maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical vulnerabilities that could let attackers run code on exposed web servers without logging in, prompting governments and companies to take websites offline while they applied patches. Precautionary shutdowns affected public services and businesses in Europe, Australia and Asia. France disabled local-government sites, the Netherlands took its DigiD digital identity portal and parliamentary sites offline, and Japanese companies suspended some online services; Wikipedia’s operator also temporarily took supporting systems offline. PHP underpins an estimated 70% of websites, though only sites running PHP on their own servers are exposed. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws using AI tools in August, and details leaked online on Oct. 20, a day before the planned patch release. Cloudflare reported millions of exploitation attempts after disclosure, while Amazon said it detected an attempt against a decoy system on Oct. 17; reports described attempts but no confirmed successful exploitation at that point. Agencies advised organizations to patch promptly or isolate vulnerable systems until they could apply the fixes.

Malicious JavaScript delivered through a website-monitoring integration sought to take over logged-in Polymarket traders’ sessions and redirect their assets, cybersecurity researchers said. Polymarket confirmed that a third-party provider was compromised and referred the incident to law enforcement, but did not publicly name the vendor. Researchers said the script read account data from browser storage, searched Polymarket’s application for its live trading client and signer, then attempted transactions using that existing access. Depending on the account type, it tried either to transfer position tokens or to sell positions and move the proceeds. Hudson Rock, which analyzed the sample, did not execute it, so its findings describe intended behavior rather than establish that every attempted transfer succeeded. Polymarket’s production build metadata showed that the DebugBear monitoring script was removed at 1:59 p.m. ET on Oct. 29, shortly before the company announced the incident, BleepingComputer reported. DebugBear separately told customers using its Real User Monitoring product to remove the embedded code and said it had brought in incident-response specialists.

items.title: [abcnews.com] U.S. home sellers cut prices and offer buyer concessions as market stalls
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

U.S. home sellers are cutting asking prices and contributing to buyers’ costs as high mortgage rates and a shortage of buyers stall home sales. In September, the median listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250, its 11th consecutive annual decline; 21% of listings had an initial price cut, the highest share in four years. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.4% this month, its highest level in nearly three years. Across the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas, sellers outnumbered buyers by about 63% last month. The number of buyers was roughly 929,000, the lowest total in records dating to 2013. Sellers are offering money toward repairs, closing costs or lower mortgage payments, but affordability pressures continue to keep prospective buyers on the sidelines.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Canadian youth climate trial tests federal emissions policy and constitutional duties
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting (insideclimatenews.org, thenarwhal.ca). Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response (winnipegfreepress.com, thestar.com). Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year (grist.org, thenarwhal.ca). Emissions gap: Canada’s 2030 target is a 40% to 45% cut from 2005 levels, but emissions had fallen only 9.5%, according to figures cited by Radio-Canada. The government has indicated it will miss the target (radio-canada.ca, blick.ch). Energy expansion: The government is supporting a liquefied natural gas terminal expansion in Kitimat that would double production capacity and pursuing the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia’s coast (insideclimatenews.org, thenarwhal.ca). Indigenous impacts: Plaintiffs describe climate threats to Indigenous food gathering and cultural practices, including reduced access to salmon, moose and berries and disruptions to outdoor ceremonies (thenarwhal.ca, radio-canada.ca). Witness evidence: The plaintiffs’ witnesses include climate scientists and specialists in children’s health, renewable energy, economics and Indigenous rights
items._kite_context:
Where: Vancouver, Canada
Perspective: Catherine Boies Parker, lawyer for the youth plaintiffs: She argued that Canada has repeatedly set insufficient emissions targets and then failed to meet them, despite decades of commitments (winnipegfreepress.com). (Winnipeg Free Press)
Perspective: Government of Canada: Counsel BJ Wray told the court that Canada is meeting its international obligations and has reduced greenhouse gas emissions since 2005 (winnipegfreepress.com). (Winnipeg Free Press)
Perspective: Ryan Ness, adaptation research director at the Canadian Climate Institute: Ness said federal climate action is not keeping pace with climate change and recent policy shifts have made Canada’s net-zero commitment harder to reach (insideclimatenews.org). (Inside Climate News)
Quote: "Canada’s evidence will show that global climate change requires a global solution" (BJ Wray, counsel for Canada’s Department of Justice, Winnipeg Free Press)
Timeline: 2020: A federal trial court dismissed the case before evidence was heard (grist.org).
Timeline: 2023: The Federal Court of Appeal allowed revised Section 7 claims to proceed (grist.org).

items.content_html:

Many Muslims saw their places of worship destroyed or abandoned during the sectarian violence of India’s partition in 1947. Now villagers of many faiths are coming together to revive them

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.

The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.

Bibi Rajinder Kaur, a Sikh, donated family land to build a mosque in her village. ‘There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,’ she says
